chapter: Alfred Williams and the Ruidoso summer
title: Alfred recalls being hired for the Ruidoso summer resort in 1936
summary: Alfred tells at length how Mr. Clayton and his partner hired his five-piece band for a summer resort in the New Mexico mountains, negotiating the pay up, and describes the band and a bear in camp.

story.theme_name: Life on the road: touring bands, buses and one-nighters
story.community_name: Life on the road: buses, trains and one-nighters

blocks.x: Would you there, Mr. Clayton, come for me to go?
Well, that must have been him.

That was, that was, uh... That name sound very familiar. No, it wasn't Clayton. It was his buddy, big six foot thin. Yeah, yeah, yeah. He had a joint in Alamogada, you see. Uh-huh. Oh, what is his name? Him and Clay Gambler, you know, you see. Oh, yeah, they was all in the rackets, man.
They was all in the rackets, man.

They was all in the... Get that guy. I thought that was him, because that's where he come from down there, you see. Uh-huh. And he built a place in Alamogada, you see. Uh-huh. Well, he couldn't make it go in Alamogada. They went up to Real Dose at the Summer Resort, you see. Uh-huh. Uh-huh. In 36, when I first got out there. Uh-huh. That was, I got out there in March, and they come around the first of June, so it opened up around there. Uh-huh. Uh-huh. Uh-huh. I was like, I don't know if I called his name. I know you'd know if I called him. That was him. Well, yeah, if I hear the name. I'm sure I would. He said he wanted a band. I'm sure I would.
He said he wanted a band.

Recognize it, yeah. Boy, we was beat. We ain't had nothing, you know. No. George was closed right through the U.S. Yeah, yeah. Well, back then was on the road. I was staying with back. Uh-huh. So, Lee was working, Lee Glover was working at the Hollywood, you know. Uh-huh. See, Hollywood was okay to sing. Yeah. He got stranded on the show with us, you know. Uh-huh. And he was singing, so Mr. Cliff, oh, I like to call that man name. Uh-huh. And they come around there and say they're looking for a band. They go ahead and they had a band on for sure. Got stranded in there, okay, so it was a pretty good band. So, Lee said, yeah. Uh-huh. Uh-huh. I said, I had a band around here, so you doing anything? Lee said, no. I said, no. He said, you go around at 906 East 2nd Street and ask for Alfred Williams. He said, now he might be in the bar at 2nd and Oregon, which I was when it's summertime, you see. Uh-huh. And that's where I was. I like to call that man name again. So, him and Mr. Clayton come around there. He said, who's named Alfred Williams around here? So, the fellas had to come next to know me, you know. Yeah. He said, he's a musician. I said, hey, he's standing over here. So, he said, can I talk to you? I said, yeah, you can talk to him. I said, come on, let's go outside. So, we went outside. He said, I'm looking for a band. And Lee Glover sent me here, told me you have a five piece band. And I'd like to take you up to Red Dosa, New Mexico. He said, summer resort will last from June the first until September the first. I said, yeah, man, that was good. I said, yeah, I don't mind. Boy, what you plan on paying? I was independent. They had a dime. Yeah. All of Australia. They had a dime. Yeah, yeah. He said, give y'all boys $10 a week, little bull and large. I said, man, don't talk. Wait a minute. I said, man, ain't no need to talking. Ain't no need to waste my time. I said, man, I make more than that right around here. Yeah. I make $2 a night around here right at home. Yeah. I said, now, that was in 1936. The thing was kind of rough, man. I needed it, you know. I said, no, we can't talk. So, he went on back around. I leave. He said, Lee, I haven't seen the fellow around there. And, man, I can't do nothing with him. He said, he was a damn good drummer. He said, but I can't do nothing with him. Look like he's kind of hard-humber, you know. Yeah. Well, he said, what you want? Mm-hmm. He told him. He said, well, oh, man. Oh, man, that wasn't nothing. No, indeed. We was hard up and kind of stranded, you know, see. So, he come back the next day. He come down there the next day by 10 o'clock that morning. I said, I hate him then when he come back. I hate him then. He said, well, Alfred, I'll come back. Now, wait a minute. Wait a minute before we fly off. Wait a minute, now. We can get together. Maybe we can get together. I said, yeah, well, let's see what kind of getting together we're going to do here. I said, now, what you putting out now? He said, I'll give you 25. I said, no, I don't want to talk about nothing. Not me. Born it so bad, I didn't know what to do, man. That man got out there, I fell off. Yeah. Yeah. I said, uh-uh, not me. I don't want to talk about it. He said, well, I'm giving you room and board. I said, man, I don't know what you're giving up in that. It's nothing there. He told us there wasn't nothing up there but white people. It's a summer resort. They didn't see no colored people. No. They had five of us and a shoeshine boy in Rio Dosa, New Mexico. That's right. That's right. That's a Indian reservation up there. Yeah. And a summer resort up in the mountains. Yeah. Off a highway, uh, what highway does that go to Roswell out of El Paso? I believe it's seven, they were one. Sixty-two. Yeah. Sixty-two go to Carl's band. Yeah. No, it's fifty-something. It's fifty-something goes to Roswell. Sixty-two go to Carl's band. Yeah. Fifty-something. Yeah. So, uh, I said, uh-huh, man. I can't believe it. I said, I know we got a good band. I know we'll make the people like it. It's a Dixieland band. The people ain't never heard nothing like this up there. He said, I know they ain't, they ain't ever had no colored band up there. They got a white band out of Dallas there. And boy, they had a fine band, I'm telling you. They had a fine band. So, I said, we can't make it, Mr. Clay. They don't need to talk. No, no, no, no, man. Not 25 hours a week. He said, I'll tell you what I'm going to do. I just want you up there. I'm going to give you 35 hours a week to roll in the bull. I said, when you want us to go? Yeah. I said, now we are ready. Yeah. He said, well, tomorrow evening. I said, we ready, man. My grip keeps back. And we want to take that. That's going to last until September the first. I took Roland, you remember Roland? Yeah. Saxophone player. An old Astieri piano player out of, what is his name? Out of Phoenix. What was his name?
What kind of piano player you called him? Huh? What did you call him?

A distillery. A distillery. A liquor. A distillery. Yeah, the stillery. Walking the stillery. Yeah. And Kemp, you remember little Kemp always called it. Oh yeah. He's a straight man, a circus man. He got to come off the circus with me. And old Willie, guitar player, keep his hair straight all the time. Yeah. What is that? Willie, what are they stillery? None of the stillery, none of them. But you know he made us some money, man. Oh sure now. He's singing all them numbers. The number was very popular there, you're my sunshine. Oh yeah. Yeah. Man, he'd get out there in that dark. It wasn't no lights. He'd put the lights out at 12 o'clock after the dance. You know what I'm saying? And he was out there just singing, you're my sunshine for the white people. And the tainer, you know. A little honey bear come up there, manning, screaming and hollering and running. But he didn't find him. He just walking by him. But scared of him, you know. And we was in our cabin, you see. We heard him. Man and Willie come tanned to that cabin. Man, it's a bear out there. It's a bear. So the next morning I went to the grocery and asked the man, say, that's a honey bear. He's coming out looking for food, you know. Yeah, so he don't buy it. Well, the only way we do. And you know Willie made some money, boy, every night when the dance would break up. We just played till 12. He's got to get the lights out at that little time. Yeah. Nothing up in the mountains, man. Three thousand feet up in the mountains. And rain damn it big.
